briefing.agreed: A bad bargain is no peace, but a war must still aim at a real one.

briefing.question: How much does a leader's private character count in public trust? And does a great founder belong to his company, or does the company have to be able to outlive him?
briefing.agreed: A strategic firm must outlive its founder; private faith can be public business.
briefing.split: Cicero, good faith; Machiavelli, results and a lasting state; Weber, charisma made routine.

briefing.question: After a victory, what does a movement owe the people who led it, and what does it owe the voters who want something new? Is a party's purpose to win the middle or to stand for something sharp?
briefing.agreed: Victory makes no leader an owner; a party needs principle and unity.
briefing.split: Aristotle, the right mean; Burke, reform not purge; Jefferson, the living; Michels, the few; Bryan, a sharp cause.

briefing.question: Can a work be separated from the person who made it? And when the two are tied together, how do we protect children without punishing someone on accusations alone?
briefing.agreed: Protect children; an accusation is not a verdict; call a removal a precaution.
briefing.split: Plato, the child first; Blackstone, Beccaria, no sentence before trial; Wilde, the work apart; Milton, no author bans.

briefing.question: Where is the line between speech that offends and speech that endangers? And should a society protect the novelist's freedom most of all, or the vulnerable neighbor's safety?
briefing.agreed: Offense is not harm; the line is incitement against identifiable people.
briefing.split: Mill, press or mob; Brandeis, imminent danger and more speech; Voltaire, tolerate opinion, curb fanaticism.

briefing.question: Who gets to be mourned in public, and are there people a community should refuse to honor? When does memory become celebration?
briefing.agreed: Mourning is a right; public honor reveals what a community loves.
briefing.split: Sophocles, burial not glory; Thucydides, honors make models; Augustine, examine loves; Mill, criticize, do not suppress.

briefing.question: Is the Church's first duty to teach the truth or to heal the wounded, and can it do one without the other?
briefing.agreed: Truth and healing are two works of one love; victims are owed justice.
briefing.split: Augustine, one root; Aquinas, mercy fulfills justice; Leo XIII, one teaching; Pascal, truth alone is an idol.

briefing.question: Does worship form us best through shared, fixed forms, or through spontaneous signs of love? And who decides what a gesture means?
briefing.agreed: Gestures teach belief; their meaning is not each person's alone.
briefing.split: Justin, the Amen; Prosper, prayer shapes belief; Augustine, indifferent customs; Calvin, few rules; Confucius, humane form.

briefing.question: Where does a religious community's freedom to preach end and the state's duty to keep the peace begin? Can a government regulate speech in a house of worship without regulating faith?
briefing.agreed: No state judgment of theology, no pulpit immunity, one rule for every faith.
briefing.split: Locke, the market test; Madison, tax benefits as a lever; Ambrose, rebuke the wrongdoer, not the neighbor.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Augustine speaks first because the report names the just-war tradition, which holds that war is justified only if it aims at a just peace, and he wrote its founding pages. Aquinas follows because he turned that teaching into tests, including right intention, which is exactly whether refusing to bargain serves peace. Thucydides is seated because the report names the Melian Dialogue as the realist case that the strong negotiate only when it helps them. Kant is seated because the report sets Perpetual Peace against that realism as the hope of diplomacy over force, and because he asked who must consent to a war. Madison closes because the report names Congress's power of the purse (Federalist No. 58) as the classic check on a president's wars, and because his Federalist No. 10 answers the second question, about judging only one's opponents. Machiavelli, also named for realism, is left off so that Thucydides carries that side alone and the table stays at five. The President, the Vice President, the Treasury Secretary, and the senators named in the report are context only.

chairs.name: Augustine
works: The City of God, Book XIX

turn.text: I never praised war as a display of strength. I said of the wise ruler that “But, say they, the wise man will wage just wars. As if he would not all the rather lament the necessity of just wars, if he remembers that he is a man” (City of God XIX.7) A war that has gone on for eight months, and that the report says is raising prices and endangering officials at home, is a necessity to be lamented, not a posture to be enjoyed. Whether a deal is needed is therefore the wrong first question. The right one is whether the war is still ordered to the peace that alone could justify it.

turn.text: I also wrote that “For every man seeks peace by waging war, but no man seeks war by making peace.” (City of God XIX.12) The supporters are right that a bargain made from weakness can reward the one who began the harm, and I would not ask the injured side to purchase quiet at any price. But to say that no deal is needed, as if peace were a concession rather than the very end of the war, inverts the order. Strength is shown in pursuing the right peace, not in declining to seek one.

chairs.modern_read: Augustine held that even a just war is a lamentable necessity, and that everyone who wages war is in fact seeking peace. He would accept that a bad bargain can reward wrongdoing, but would not treat refusing to negotiate as strength in itself, since peace is the only purpose that can justify the war.

chairs.name: Thomas Aquinas

turn.text: Augustine names the end; I would add a test for the means. Among the conditions of a just war I placed this one: “Thirdly, it is necessary that the belligerents should have a rightful intention, so that they intend the advancement of good, or the avoidance of evil.” (Summa Theologica II-II, Q. 40, Art. 1) Sanctions, pressure, even the refusal of a particular offer, can serve that intention if they are meant to bring the enemy to a just settlement. They fail it if they are kept up for their own sake, or to win a quarrel at home.

But I would ask those who say the country does not need any deal what peace they are aiming at, and by what road. If no road is offered, the intention is in doubt, and Augustine's warning applies: the war has stopped serving its end.

He would allow refusing a bad bargain but would ask what peace the refusal is meant to reach, and would doubt the intention if no path to peace is offered.

He would reject a sham deal but would treat voters and their representatives weighing the war's costs as the proper check that keeps a republic from making war lightly.

chairs.name: James Madison

turn.text: Kant has led us to the purse, which is where I would end. I described it as the people's chief instrument: “This power over the purse may, in fact, be regarded as the most complete and effectual weapon with which any constitution can arm the immediate representatives of the people, for obtaining a redress of every grievance, and for carrying into effect every just and salutary measure.” (Federalist No. 58) The progressives who want the December bill to bar money for combat are using that weapon; those who warn of a shutdown are pointing out its cost. Both are acting within the design. The purse was given to the House precisely so that the representatives could say yes or no to what the executive asks.

turn.text: I would not separate the private man from the public trust as neatly as some wish. I wrote that “The foundation of justice, moreover, is good faith--that is, truth and fidelity to promises and agreements.” (De Officiis I.vii.23) An affair is a broken promise before it is anything else. That does not prove a betrayal of the country, and the report is careful to say no spying has been confirmed. But when the private faithlessness was with someone suspected of serving a foreign power, and the man holds the keys to a strategic art, the city has a fair reason to ask whether good faith holds elsewhere.

turn.text: Machiavelli's last point is the one I spent years on. I distinguished authority that rests on tradition, on rules, and on charisma, the extraordinary gifts a following attributes to one person (Economy and Society, paraphrased). Founders of new enterprises often rule by the third kind. Their followers believe in them personally, which is why one side says his grasp is impossible to replicate. But charisma is unstable by nature. It must be proved again and again, and when it is handed on, by designation or by heredity, it is already being changed into something more ordinary (Economy and Society, paraphrased).

sittings.why_these_chairs: Aristotle speaks first because the report names his golden mean and the case for moderation, and his Politics argues that the best community rests on the middle rank. Burke follows because the report names his prudence and respect for experienced leadership, and because he gave the classic definition of a party. Jefferson is seated because the report names his claim that the earth belongs to the living, each generation's right to govern itself. Michels is seated because the report names his iron law of oligarchy, that parties built for the many tend to be run by the few; his Political Parties is not on the shelf in a fetched public-domain text, so he is paraphrased. Bryan closes because the report names the populist tradition from the Gracchi to him, and his Cross of Gold speech is the classic American case for a sharp party of the many. The Gracchi are left off because they left no writings; Plutarch's account of them would make a biographer the chair. opening.text: Tonight's subject: who gets to be mourned in public, are there people a community should refuse to honor, and when does memory become celebration? The report gives one side as critics, who say honoring the planner of the October 7 massacre in a sacred Latino tradition, in a city-owned park, glorifies terrorism and makes Jewish neighbors feel unsafe, and that a cultural center whose stated mission is goodwill and understanding has lost sight of it. sittings.headline: Pope Leo, home in Peru, denounces machismo and tells bishops to face abuse with truth and justice
sittings.question: Is the Church's first duty to teach the truth or to heal the wounded, and can it do one without the other?

setup.text: On his first full day in Peru, where he served for two decades, the Peruvian-born pope told 40,000 people in Lima that violence against women continues to wound all of humanity, urged bishops to respond to clergy-abuse victims with truth and justice and to combine doctrinal fidelity with pastoral closeness, and spoke up for marriage between a man and a woman and for the unborn. sittings.why_these_chairs: Augustine speaks first because the report names his short precept, love and do what you will, as the root of both correction and compassion, and because the pope belongs to the order that bears his name. Aquinas follows because he wrote the classic account of how justice and mercy fit together, and because the report names natural-law teaching on marriage and life. Leo XIII is seated because the report names Rerum Novarum as the start of the social teaching that holds the dignity of the person demands social justice. Pascal closes because his warning that truth without charity becomes an idol is the sharpest statement of the pairing the report names from John 1:14, which the moderator reads. Later popes and the Second Vatican Council's documents are in copyright and are not seated; the pope himself and the bishops named in the report are context only.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: is the Church's first duty to teach the truth or to heal the wounded, and can it do one without the other? The report gives one side as Catholics who stress the Church's social witness, who hear a pastor naming real wounds, since femicides in Peru rose 44 percent between 2016 and 2024 and abuse victims need justice, not silence, and who see the Church at its best defending poor, Indigenous and Afro-Peruvian women and humbly owning its infidelities. The other side is Catholics who stress doctrinal clarity, who point to his defense of marriage, the unborn and the family, argue that renewal in a shrinking church comes from clear teaching and sacraments rather than social commentary, and warn against reading the trip as purely about social justice. Both camps quote his line about pairing doctrine with closeness. The report names the Gospel's pairing: “And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.” (John 1:14) Augustine, the report begins with your precept. closing.text: Where they agreed: teaching the truth and healing the wounded are not rival duties but two works of one love, and victims of abuse are owed justice, not only closeness. turn.text: My precept is often quoted as a license. It was the opposite. I said: “Love, and do what you will: whether you hold your peace, through love hold your peace; whether you cry out, through love cry out; whether you correct, through love correct; whether you spare, through love do you spare” (Homilies on the First Epistle of John, Homily 7, §8) I gave it in a sermon about correction: a father who strikes and a kidnapper who caresses can look alike, and only the root tells them apart. Love is not the alternative to truth. It is the root from which both the hard word and the gentle one must grow.

Justice, I wrote, “justice is a habit whereby a man renders to each one his due by a constant and perpetual will” (Summa Theologica II-II, Q. 58, Art. 1) Victims of abuse are owed truth and justice; that is not optional pastoral kindness but a debt. A church that offered them closeness without justice would be offering mercy in place of what it owes, and that is not mercy.

The social camp is right that mercy toward the poor and wounded is the fullness of that justice. Taken apart, each becomes a counterfeit of itself.

turn.text: Leo shows that the two halves belong to one teaching. I would warn what happens when one half is made into the whole. I wrote that “We make an idol of truth itself; for truth apart from charity is not God, but His image and idol, which we must neither love nor worship” (Pensées, 581 (Trotter)) A church that preaches doctrine as a banner while victims wait for justice has made an idol of its truth. But the reverse danger is real too: a charity that will not say what is true about the person, the family, or sin is not charity, only sentiment.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: does worship form us best through shared, fixed forms or through spontaneous signs of love, and who decides what a gesture means? The report gives one side as supporters who welcome the clarity: the liturgy belongs to the whole Church, not to any one parish, gestures carry meaning, and when the priest prays for the people, copying his posture blurs his role, so following the Missal faithfully is a form of humility. turn.text: Augustine treats such gestures as indifferent. I mostly agree, but I would not call them meaningless. I wrote that “The corporeal gestures usually observed in prayer, such as kneeling and uncovering the head, are customs designed to increase our reverence of God.” (Institutes III.xx.33) A gesture is a servant of reverence; it is right when it helps and wrong when it distracts. The question is, whether it be a human tradition, which every one is at liberty to reject or neglect. turn.text: Madison guards the pulpit from the state. I used a bishop's authority against an emperor, after soldiers under his order massacred the people of Thessalonica. I told him “I dare not offer the sacrifice if you intend to be present.” (Letter 51, §13) and I reminded him of the prophet who came to David with the word “And Nathan said to David, Thou art the man.” (2 Samuel 12:7) The preacher's freedom to denounce injustice, even by the powerful, is ancient and holy. The prophet Amos asked that “But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.” (Amos 5:24) No regulator should silence that.

I wrote “I have written this, not in order to confound you, but that the examples of these kings may stir you up to put away this sin from your kingdom” (Letter 51, §11) and near the close I added “I am writing with my own hand that which you alone may read.” (Letter 51, §14) The prophetic word aims at the repentance of the wrongdoer, not the inflaming of a crowd against neighbors who did not commit the wrong.
